common_name: Tone Wase Persimmon (Early-Ripening Hiratanenashi Bud-Sport Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun once frost danger has passed, giving it the deep, well-drained soil typical of oriental persimmons.

directions: Tone Wase is a naturally occurring bud-sport mutation of the astringent Japanese cultivar Hiratanenashi, selected and named for ripening roughly one to two weeks ahead of its parent. Like other astringent kaki, the oblong-conical fruit carries very high sugar content but must be fully softened, frozen, or gas-treated to remove tannins before it becomes palatable and sweet. Japanese growers have used Tone Wase in forced early-season culture because of its reliable early-ripening window, though home growers can simply let fruit color and soften on the tree into fall. Give it the same deep, well-drained soil and full-sun siting used for other oriental persimmons, and expect a vigorous, upright tree similar in habit to Hiratanenashi.
sources: Journal of the Japanese Society for Horticultural Science

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, giving it room to develop into a large, long-lived specimen.

directions: Yokono is a traditional Japanese astringent persimmon cultivar valued for its large, orange-red fruit and dependable heavy annual cropping. The astringent flesh must be fully ripened to a soft, jelly-like texture or treated to remove tannins before eating, after which it develops rich, honeyed sweetness well suited to drying as hoshigaki. Trees tend to shed a portion of their developing fruit through the growing season, so thinning is rarely needed, and the foliage turns attractive shades of orange and red in autumn before leaf drop. Site it in full sun with deep, well-drained soil like other kaki persimmons, and expect a long-lived, self-fruitful tree that stores its harvested fruit well.
sources: Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun once frost danger has passed; train to an open form in deep, well-drained soil.

directions: Imoto is a non-astringent kaki persimmon selected as a strain within the Fuyu group, producing flattened, seedless fruit that can be eaten crisp like an apple as soon as it colors, without any need to wait for softening. It typically ripens a touch earlier than standard Fuyu, coloring up in early to mid fall, and regional trials have found it holds its leaves and crop reasonably well through early freeze events. The tree is self-fruitful and sets a full crop without a separate pollinator, making it a reliable single-tree choice for home orchards. Grow it exactly as you would Fuyu, in full sun and deep, well-drained soil, training to an open form for easy harvest.

common_name: Hana Gosho Persimmon (Compact Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in loamy, moist but well-drained soil; this compact kaki tolerates partial shade better than most persimmons.

directions: Hana Gosho is a non-astringent kaki persimmon bearing medium to large, flat-to-conic orange-red fruit that can be sliced and eaten firm, like an apple or tomato, as soon as it colors in fall. The vigorous tree grows upright on a strong scaffold to a modest 12 to 15 feet, noticeably smaller than many kaki cultivars, making it a good fit for home orchards with limited space. Although it fruits as a female-type tree, it produces a scattering of male flowers most seasons, and fruit set and size tend to improve when another kaki cultivar grows within pollinating range. The tree adapts to a wide range of well-drained soils and tolerates drought once established, though root suckers should be pruned away periodically.

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting on a sturdy permanent trellis or pergola in spring in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Hortgem Tahi is a New Zealand-bred Actinidia arguta selection developed by Plant & Food Research (formerly HortResearch) and marketed commercially under the Nergi brand alongside its sibling selection Hortgem Rua. It produces small, smooth, hairless-skinned kiwiberries that can be eaten whole, skin and all, with sweet, aromatic green flesh and none of the fuzzy texture of standard kiwifruit. As a dioecious female vine it needs a compatible hardy kiwi male growing within range to set fruit, and like other arguta types it should be trained onto a sturdy permanent trellis or pergola. Harvested berries soften and lose quality quickly after picking, so plan to eat or process fruit within a few days of harvest.

common_name: Hortgem Rua Kiwiberry (Red-Centered Nergi Hardy Kiwi)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting on a sturdy permanent trellis in spring in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Hortgem Rua is the red-fleshed companion selection to Hortgem Tahi, bred in New Zealand by Plant & Food Research and sold together under the Nergi kiwiberry brand. Its small, oblong, hairless green-skinned fruit develops a distinctive red-blushed center in the flesh as it ripens, paired with the same sweet, aromatic flavor typical of hardy kiwiberries. Being a female clone, it requires a male Actinidia arguta vine nearby for pollination and will not set a crop on its own. Grow it on a strong trellis in full sun with well-drained soil, and harvest promptly once berries soften since, like other kiwiberries, they do not hold well after picking.

common_name: Vitakola Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Large-Fruited Kolomikta Kiwi)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting against a trellis or fence in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Vitakola is a Czech-bred female selection of Actinidia kolomikta prized for unusually large fruit, up to about an inch and three-quarters long, that ripens greenish-yellow with a sweet flavor often compared to pineapple and raspberry. It is exceptionally cold hardy, reportedly tolerating temperatures well below zero Fahrenheit once established, making it a good fit for far northern gardens where standard kiwifruit cannot survive. As a female clone it needs a male kolomikta pollinator such as Adam growing nearby, and typically begins cropping around its third or fourth year. Give it a site with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since kolomikta foliage and fruit quality suffer under intense all-day sun.

common_name: Dr Szymanowski Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Partially Self-Fertile Kolomikta Kiwi)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting on a trellis or fence in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun.

directions: Dr Szymanowski is a Polish-bred female selection of Actinidia kolomikta notable for producing elongated, sweet kiwiberries and for being partially self-fertile, meaning a lone vine can set some fruit without a male pollinator present. Yields and fruit set still improve markedly when a male kolomikta vine grows nearby, so most growers pair it with a pollinator for a full crop. Like other arctic kiwi selections, it is extremely cold hardy and suited to northern gardens, with ornamental spring foliage that can show pink and white variegation on vigorous shoots. Train it on a trellis or fence in part shade to full sun and provide humus-rich, well-drained soil for best growth.
